title: Citizen 13660: An Artist's Internment Diary
author: Miné Okubo
citation: Okubo, Miné. Citizen 13660. Columbia University Press, 1946.

sections.heading: Evacuation and The Number 13660

epigraph.quote: I had become a number: Citizen 13660. My name, my privacy, and my constitutional rights were stripped away overnight.

paragraphs: Miné Okubo was an accomplished American-born artist and University of California, Berkeley graduate when President Franklin D. Roosevelt issued Executive Order 9066 in February 1942. Without charges, hearings, or trials, more than 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry—two-thirds of them American citizens—were forcibly ordered to evacuate their West Coast homes.

Every family was assigned a family number; baggage and personal identification were stamped with the number 13660. Miné and her brother were sent first to Tanforan Assembly Center, a converted racetrack in San Bruno, California, where families were housed in smelly horse stalls hastily swept out and covered with whitewash. Rather than succumbing to despair, Miné resolved to document every aspect of camp life through sketches and concise diary entries.

sections.heading: Topaz, Utah: Dust Storms, Barbed Wire, and Dignity

epigraph.quote: The camera was forbidden, but the eye and the sketchpad could not be confiscated.

paragraphs: In late 1942, Okubo was transferred to the Central Utah Relocation Center in the arid desert of Topaz, Utah. There, behind barbed wire fences guarded by armed soldiers in watchtowers, internees endured freezing winters, scorching summers, and violent dust storms that coated bedding, food, and clothes in fine alkali powder.

Through her drawings and writing, Okubo captured the quiet heroism, humor, and communal solidarity of the internees. They planted gardens, built makeshift schools, organized sports leagues, and cared for one another. Published in 1946, Citizen 13660 became the first published firsthand account of Japanese-American internment by an internee, serving as an indelible testament to the fragility of civil liberties during wartime.
